sections.title: Front matter

summary.text: The front matter of the UNAIDS/WHO Guiding principles on ethical issues in HIV surveillance (2013), with cataloguing data, ISBN and copyright notice. It includes acknowledgements and a table of contents. The contents run from ethical guidance and the history of research ethics through data collection and obligations to disseminate data and intervene, to conclusions and references.

sections.title: Notification: name-based surveillance

summary.text: Gives guidance that name-based HIV case reporting is justified only with strict confidentiality and use solely for public health, and that data be shared only with adequate security and the stricter privacy standard.

sections.extract: Notification: name-based surveillance Guidance 1. Name-based HIV case reporting (as contrasted with anonymous or coded reporting) can be justified only if data can be maintained in a confidential manner. The data should be used only for purposes related to public health (and not for discrimination or criminalization). sections.title: Informed consent

summary.text: Sets out guidance on informed consent for HIV surveillance, requiring ethics review of research surveillance and listing what participants must be told, including risks, benefits and freedom to decline. It also addresses community consultation and opt-out approaches, citing the Kenya AIDS Indicator Survey.

sections.extract: Informed consent Guidance 3. All surveillance classified as research should be reviewed by ethical review boards (or human subjects’ research oversight committees) to ensure that the consent process fully informs potential participants about:   the public health goals of the study,   their freedom to decline to participate,   the need to ask sensitive questions about sex and other behaviours linked to HIV

sections.title: Vulnerable populations

summary.text: Gives guidance on involving vulnerable populations in HIV surveillance, including adolescents, who may consent from around 15 while younger children need parental consent and support services. It also covers groups such as sex workers, people who use drugs and men who have sex with men, stressing protection from legal harm and limits of confidentiality.

sections.extract: Vulnerable populations Guidance 7. Understanding the patterns of sexual and drug-using behaviour among adolescents justifies studies involving adolescents. However, they must understand the risks and benefits of participating in surveillance activities. Explaining the risks and benefits is often possible among those aged 15–18 years.3 Children below the age of 15 years, who lack the capacity to understand the risks

sections.title: Unlinked anonymous testing (UAT)

summary.text: Gives guidance on unlinked anonymous HIV testing, which should be used only when other data cannot meet surveillance needs, be reviewed for ethical and epidemiological soundness and offer participants a way to learn their status.

sections.extract: Unlinked anonymous testing (UAT) Guidance 13. Unlinked anonymous testing (UAT) occurs when persons are tested for HIV but the test and results are not linked to any identifying information. The participants are not provided with their results. UAT is often done without informed consent. It should be used for surveillance only when data from clinical settings and other studies cannot provide the information necessary

sections.title: Data use

summary.text: Gives guidance that HIV surveillance is justified only if it helps prevention or directs resources, that results must be shared with communities, and that people at risk should be referred to services or the project should advocate for them.

sections.extract: Data use Guidance 17. Surveillance efforts can be justified only if they will help prevent the spread of HIV or will be used for directing resources to those already infected. When there is resistance to effective interventions or resources are scarce, surveillance may be used as a basis for advocacy and empowering the most vulnerable populations. Guidance 18. The results of surveillance must always be communicated

sections.title: Introduction

summary.text: Introduces the need for ethical guidelines for second generation HIV surveillance, which since 2000 has added behavioural data and focused on populations at higher risk. It argues that accurate surveillance is essential to control the epidemic and that there may be a duty to conduct it. It identifies the intended users, including ministries, NGOs, community advisory boards and ethics committees.

sections.extract: Why do we need ethical guidelines for second generation surveillance? In 2000, the World Health Organization (WHO) and Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS) published the Guidelines for second generation HIV surveillance.(1) The guidelines are a series of modules released over the past decade, designed to address the complexity of different HIV epidemic contexts and meet the planning needs of national

sections.title: Overview of national and international ethical guidelines on surveillance

summary.text: Reviews national and international ethical guidelines relevant to surveillance, tracing medical ethics from the Nuremberg Code through phases of articulation and oversight following scandals like the Tuskegee study. It notes how guidelines treat epidemiological studies and the use of existing records and biological specimens.

sections.extract: Overview of national and international ethical guidelines on surveillance The modern era of medical ethics began with the promulgation of the Nuremberg Code in 1947. Nuremberg marked the first of three major phases in the evolution of medical ethics. sections.title: Medical ethics and the ethics of epidemiological research: a literature review

summary.text: Reviews literature on medical and epidemiological research ethics, noting that Nuremberg and Helsinki prioritized the individual over society with no exceptions to consent. It describes how later guidance, including CIOMS, adapted these principles to population research and stressed building ethical review capacity in host countries.

sections.title: Research, practice and surveillance

summary.text: Discusses the distinction between research and practice, from the Declaration of Helsinki onward, and the difficulty of classifying surveillance. It concludes that the ethical guidelines should apply to second generation surveillance either way, with mechanisms needed if it is treated as practice.

sections.extract: Research, practice and surveillance With so much attention devoted to the standards that ought to govern medical research and to the mechanisms that could best ensure ethical oversight, it was deemed crucial to distinguish that domain of clinical practice which was not subject to the same regulatory norms. sections.title: Public health and mandatory notification

summary.text: Examines mandatory public health notification, under which health workers must report identifiable cases to authorities by law, often without consent. It discusses how ethics bodies have accepted such breaches of consent for public health while recognizing deep disagreement in the case of HIV.

sections.extract: Public health and mandatory notification In many nations, there is a long history of governmentally mandated and conducted public health surveillance that has been the primary source of data relevant to the understanding of patterns of morbidity and mortality, or the evaluation of efforts designed to limit the impact of disease outbreaks and epidemics. sections.title: Data collection for HIV surveillance

summary.text: Traces the history of name-based disease notification in the United States and Europe, rooted in nineteenth-century epidemic control and vital registration. It describes the shift from AIDS to HIV case reporting and the debate over names versus coded identifiers, including in resource-limited settings. It ends by discussing privacy when linking HIV data with other databases and restating guidance on name-based reporting and data sharing.

sections.extract: Public health surveillance: the role of mandatory notification Surveillance was the foundation on which the new public health was built, not only in the United States but also in Europe. The move toward the reporting of disease by name to health officials in the United States was paralleled in Europe, driven in part by the cholera epidemics of the nineteenth century. sections.title: Individuals, local context and the consent process

summary.text: Discusses consent in behavioural studies within second generation HIV surveillance, which gather highly sensitive data on sexual practices and drug use from groups such as sex workers, men who have sex with men and people who inject drugs. It argues that subject selection must be epidemiologically justified so vulnerable groups are not unduly burdened. Participants must give fully informed, affirmative opt-in consent that takes account of local language, beliefs and history. Opt-out procedures are judged unacceptable for face-to-face studies.

sections.title: Role of community consultation in the consent process

summary.text: Argues that, alongside individual consent, consultation with community representatives is vital for HIV surveillance, citing the Nuffield Council and the US National Bioethics Advisory Commission. It notes that community permission cannot replace individual consent and gives the Kenya AIDS Indicator Survey as an example where late consultation lowered participation.

sections.extract: As noted, researchers are obliged to protect the rights of individual subjects through an informed consent process. Both for surveillance involving contact with individuals as well as the investigation of already existing records, as discussed above, an additional step will prove vital: consultation with those who may represent the community at large. sections.title: Unique issues of consent with minors and the role of parents in the consent process

summary.text: Examines consent for minors in HIV surveillance, where parental consent and child assent may conflict with the need to interview adolescents about sexual behaviour, citing CIOMS guidance. It sets out conditions under which adolescents might participate without parental permission and stresses access to counselling and support services.

sections.extract: The very basic principles of research ethics, which seek to protect the right of individuals to not participate in investigations if that is their choice, also require the protection of vulnerable individuals who may not have the psychological or legal capacity to choose. sections.title: Impact of social context on the capacity for consent: prisons and clinical settings

summary.text: Explains that patients in clinics and prisoners may feel unable to refuse surveillance studies, fearing their care or treatment will suffer. It recommends community consultation, having staff not involved in care obtain consent, and special scrutiny by ethics committees of prisoners' voluntary choice.

sections.extract: Settings in which individuals receive medical care, such as prenatal clinics, STI clinics, TB treatment centres and hospitals, provide a natural context for second generation surveillance. Inevitably, patients who are recruited to studies may believe that they have no alternative but to agree to participate. sections.title: Unique issues of consent with vulnerable populations

summary.text: Discusses how payments or services may unduly induce poor or marginalised people to join surveillance, citing CIOMS guidelines and noting the limits of local ethics review. It stresses informed, voluntary consent, enforceable confidentiality and clearly stated limits to confidentiality for the most-at-risk populations.

sections.extract: The problem of the coercive impact of undue inducements extends beyond prison populations. In poor or marginalized populations, small offers or payments to potential participants in second generation surveillance may be hard to refuse. sections.title: Unique issues of consent with women

summary.text: Considers consent for women in societies where men are expected to decide, noting CIOMS's position that husbands may not consent on women's behalf and the NBAC's narrow exception allowing supplemental male permission. It concludes that a woman's own consent is required and that lack of male approval must never exclude her.

sections.extract: The 2002 CIOMS International ethical guidelines for biomedical research involving human subjects maintained that husbands or heads of households may not consent on behalf of women. Nonetheless, in many societies, the father, husband or family head is expected to make all decisions regarding sensitive family issues. Women and other family members who fail to submit to male authority may be subject to domestic

sections.title: Confidentiality

summary.text: Sets out the ethical and practical reasons for protecting confidentiality in HIV surveillance, citing CIOMS and the Nuffield Council and a study in Côte d'Ivoire where fear of disclosure lowered testing. It addresses data security and legal reporting requirements, stating that participants must be told of any limits to confidentiality.

sections.extract: As noted, CIOMS, in its 2002 revision of International ethical guidelines for biomedical research involving human subjects, established an obligation on the part of investigators to safeguard the confidentiality of subjects’ research data. sections.title: Anonymous unlinked surveillance

summary.text: Traces the history and ethics of unlinked anonymous HIV testing of blood collected for other purposes, which became the backbone of surveillance in generalised epidemics. It describes how US authorities and a 1985 Hastings Center group judged it ethical, and how WHO's 1989 guidance supported it. The section then covers growing debate as treatment became available and the case for informing people of their status grew. It concludes that women in antenatal clinic surveillance must also be referred to prevention of mother-to-child transmission services.

sections.extract: Anonymous unlinked surveillance With the identification of HIV in 1984, it became clear that an understanding of the dimensions of the AIDS epidemic would require more than a careful detailing of the incidence and prevalence of overt symptoms of the disease. sections.title: Individual consent to blood drawn specifically for HIV surveillance

summary.text: Discusses consent for blood drawn specifically for HIV testing in household surveys, where direct contact with participants raises the question of how they should learn their results. It concludes that participants must be offered the chance to learn their results through survey teams, mobile units or local clinics.

sections.extract: While much of the discussion on UAT had focused on ANCs and the needs and claims of women, there was also increasing uncertainty about the ethics of UAT in population-based household surveys. sections.title: Obligation to use data

summary.text: Argues that surveillance, like research, is justified only if it benefits the populations studied, citing the Declaration of Helsinki and CIOMS, and that ethics committees should consider how data will be used. It notes that surveillance can support advocacy for vulnerable groups.

sections.extract: Obligation to use data There is now international consensus that research in a given population is justified only if the results of studies will provide benefit to the populations from which participants are drawn. Surveillance activities have always been justified in terms of the population-level benefits that would follow. sections.title: Obligation to disseminate data

summary.text: Sets out the ethical obligation to share surveillance findings with participants and communities, citing NBAC, international researchers and the Nuffield Council. It adds guidance that, when results could harm the population, risks should be minimised in consultation with community representatives.

sections.extract: Obligation to disseminate data Dissemination of findings represents a benefit to which the participants in surveillance-related activities have an ethical claim. sections.title: Obligation to intervene at the community level

summary.text: Notes that surveillance teams may not be able to ensure services such as condoms or needle exchange, and gives guidance that investigators should agree in advance with community boards and ethics committees what advocacy role they will play.

sections.extract: Obligation to intervene at the community level Researchers and others who conduct surveillance may not be able to ensure that vulnerable communities have access to the services that surveillance reveals would be helpful in preventing the spread of HIV, such as condoms, supportive services for women or needle exchange programmes. sections.title: Obligation to intervene at the individual level

summary.text: Discusses obligations when interviews reveal that participants are at risk from lack of information, lack of services or coercive partners, recommending referral to appropriate services. Where referrals are impossible, it says the project itself should advocate for services with ethical oversight bodies.

sections.extract: Obligation to intervene at the individual level Those conducting integrated behavioural and biological studies and surveillance activities may, during the course of the interview, become aware that a participant is placing himself or herself at risk because of a lack of information about how HIV is acquired and transmitted, limited access to preventive services or psychosocial stressors. sections.title: Summary and Conclusions: ethical implications of type of epidemic

summary.text: Concludes that there is an ethical obligation to conduct HIV surveillance because of its potential to prevent disease and death, but notes the challenge of providing ethical oversight for surveillance outside research. It stresses confidentiality and consent given stigma and discrimination linked to HIV. It then explains how ethical concerns differ between low-level, concentrated and generalised epidemics.
